options: The higher of an asset's fair value less costs to sell, or its value in use
The lower of cost and net book value
The amount recovered from an insurance claim only
questions.explain: Recoverable amount is defined, under the IAS 36 framework, as the higher of fair value less costs to sell and value in use.

questions.q: When is an asset considered impaired?
options: When its carrying amount is lower than its recoverable amount
When its recoverable amount is less than its carrying amount
When it is placed in service
When it is reclassified into a different category
questions.explain: An asset is impaired when its recoverable amount falls below its current carrying amount (net book value).

questions.q: A packaging line has a $280,000 carrying amount and a $190,000 recoverable amount. What is the impairment loss?
questions.explain: $280,000 - $190,000 = $90,000, the impairment loss recognized as an expense while the carrying value is written down to $190,000.

options: The routine passage of a depreciation period
An indicator such as obsolescence, damage, or a market shift suggesting the asset's value no longer reflects reality
The asset reaching the end of its scheduled life
questions.explain: Impairment is triggered by specific adverse indicators, not by the routine, planned passage of depreciation.

questions.q: How does impairment differ from revaluation?
options: Impairment is a deliberate upward restatement; revaluation is always a write-down
Impairment is an unplanned, indicator-driven write-down; revaluation is a deliberate policy restatement that can go either direction
They are the same process with different names
Revaluation only applies to retired assets
questions.explain: Impairment responds to an unplanned adverse event and is almost always a loss, while revaluation is a deliberate, policy-driven restatement that can increase or decrease value.
